sections.h2: Which offices handle property tax in Grant County, KY?
sections.html:
A Grant County tax bill passes through three counters. The PVA decides what each parcel is worth. The sheriff takes payment on the current year. The county clerk takes over whatever bills remain after mid-April. Rates come from the levying bodies themselves: the fiscal court, the school system, and any city or special district that taxes the parcel.

The PVA keeps an office in the Williamstown courthouse, 101 North Main Street, and the phone is (859) 824-6511. The sheriff works from 212 Barnes Road, Suite A, weekdays from 8 to 4, and answers at (859) 824-3333. Checks can be mailed to PO Box 235, Dry Ridge, KY 41035. The county directory sends delinquent-bill questions to the clerk at (859) 824-3321.

City tax bills never go through the sheriff. Williamstown, Dry Ridge, Corinth and Crittenden each bill their own, so a municipal charge on a closing statement is a question for that city hall.

sections.h2: What is the payment calendar for a Grant County tax bill?
sections.html:
The sheriff mails bills and posts them online on October 1, then takes payment until April 15. Splitting a bill into two installments is not allowed. Cards work, with a processing charge from the card company, and a mail-in payer who wants a receipt encloses a stamped return envelope.

Grant County Sheriff's posted schedule for current-year bills (source: Grant County Sheriff's Office, tax collection page)
Payment madeResult
Oct. 1 through Nov. 1Two percent off the bill
Nov. 2 through Dec. 31Bill at face value
All of JanuaryFive percent added
Feb. 1 through Apr. 15Twenty-one percent added, as posted
After Apr. 15County Clerk takes over the bill

The state law behind this calendar, KRS 134.015, sets a 10 percent penalty for anything paid after January. The sheriff's 21 percent for February through April 15 runs higher than that, so request an itemized payoff in writing if a contract depends on the number.

sections.h2: Why did my Grant County tax bill arrive in the seller's name?
sections.html:
The sheriff bills whoever was listed as owner on January 1. Buy in spring and the year's first bill still carries the previous owner's name. Deed transfers never reach the sheriff, which leaves the seller to pass the bill on.

  • Write the split of that year's bill into the purchase agreement, since the county does not apportion it.
  • Have the deed carry a c/o address for the buyer, as KRS 382.135 demands.
  • After recording, call the PVA and confirm the mailing address now on file.

If the closing agent pays the open bill from the seller's proceeds, the settlement statement should show it on a line of its own.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Grant County assessment?
sections.html:
Nobody can file an appeal without first sitting down with the PVA or a deputy, which makes that office your first stop. Then comes a 13-day public viewing of the roll, starting the first Monday of May.

  • At the conference, the PVA walks through the method behind your value and keeps a written record.
  • Hand the written appeal to the Clerk before the office closes on the workday after the viewing period ends.
  • Collect proof: nearby sales, contractor bids, photos of damage, insurance papers, cost of construction.
  • Attend the board hearing, which falls within five weeks of the window closing. A no-show forfeits further review by the state Claims Commission.

An appeal without documents is denied by the board. Should bills go out before the board decides, your own figure is billed for now. A higher final value brings a second bill for the difference.

sections.h2: Is there a homestead exemption in Grant County?
sections.html:
Yes. For 2025-2026, owners who have reached 65 or are totally disabled may deduct $49,100 from the assessment. A Grant County house assessed at $250,000 would be taxed on $200,900.

Applications are made at the PVA, and the sheriff's office refers anyone asking about it there. A birth certificate, driver's license or passport proves age. Disability filers renew yearly, with two groups spared that chore: veterans rated service-connected, and anyone holding a permanent-disability finding from Social Security or the state retirement system.

Notify the PVA at sale so the deduction leaves your old address, and a qualifying buyer can apply separately.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid Grant County taxes when I sell?
sections.html:
Back taxes ride with the parcel. The sheriff deals only with the current year, so a bill that crosses April 15 lands with the Clerk, and a lien is recorded against the property. A buyer inherits the lien, which can last 11 years (KRS 134.420).

Costs climb in steps. The state's worked example begins with a $1,000 bill. It arrives at the Clerk as a $1,254 certificate, and by the time the county attorney's first notice has gone out the payoff reads $1,611.30, after monthly interest, two commissions, postage and a $10 lien fee.

An auction of the certificate can happen from day 90 to day 135 after transfer, and the winning bidder may tack on charges. Get a Clerk's quote on the payoff before the sign goes up. With a cash buyer, the lien is paid at closing out of the price.

sections.h2: What else should a Grant County seller know about the area?
sections.html:
Grant County lies in northern Kentucky inside the Cincinnati metropolitan area. It was carved from Pendleton County in 1820 and has 258 square miles of land. Williamstown holds the courthouse, while Dry Ridge, Corinth and Crittenden complete the list of cities. Families here send children to Grant County Schools or to Williamstown Independent Schools, and the Ark Encounter in Williamstown brings in visitors from across the region. Seven counties border it: Boone, Kenton, Pendleton, Harrison, Scott, Owen and Gallatin. Public transit is limited to demand-response service from Senior Services of Northern Kentucky, and county voters approved full alcohol sales in a December 2015 special election.

Growth is the main story here. The census counted 9,999 residents in 1970, 22,384 in 2000 and 24,941 in 2020, and the 1939 courthouse in Williamstown has since been joined by a judicial center that opened in April 2010. Census QuickFacts reports:

  • A 2025 population of 26,181, which is 5.0 percent above the 2020 base.
  • Homeowners make up 75.1 percent of households, and the median home value is $209,500.
  • Median household income of $69,178 and a mean commute of 26.9 minutes.
  • Median gross rent of $862 and 110 building permits in 2025, with 96.7 people per square mile.

A cash purchase closes as-is, which can suit an owner with repairs waiting or a balance outstanding.

faqs.q: Who takes property tax payments in Grant County, KY?
faqs.a: The sheriff's office handles it, either at 212 Barnes Road, Suite A in Williamstown or through the mail to PO Box 235, Dry Ridge. After April 15, the County Clerk collects.

faqs.q: When does the Grant County early-payment discount end?
faqs.a: On November 1. Paying the whole bill from October 1 through that day takes two percent off, and face value applies from November 2.

faqs.q: Can a Grant County tax bill be paid in two installments?
faqs.a: No. The sheriff requires full payment of each bill, so pick a payment window you can cover in one go.

faqs.q: What does the homestead deduction take off a Grant County house?
faqs.a: It removes $49,100 from the assessment for 2025-2026. Filing is with the PVA at (859) 824-6511, and the owner must be 65 or older or totally disabled.

faqs.q: Must back taxes be settled before I list a Grant County house?
faqs.a: They can wait. The lien follows the parcel and is settled from the sale proceeds. Call the Clerk at (859) 824-3321 for the amount so your title agent can plan.
